Let

\[
\alpha=a(1-q+qr),\qquad \beta=q(1-r),\qquad \gamma=r.
\]

Then the center is

\[
\boxed{
Z(R)=k\bigl[a,q,r,\ \beta X-\alpha Y,\ \gamma X-\alpha Z,\ \gamma Y-\beta Z\bigr].
}
\]

Equivalently, since \(q=b+a^2\) and \(r=c+ab\),

\[
\boxed{
Z(R)=k\Bigl[
a,b,c,\ 
q(1-r)X-a(1-q+qr)Y,\ 
rX-a(1-q+qr)Z,\ 
rY-q(1-r)Z
\Bigr].
}
\]

These three nontrivial central generators satisfy the relation

\[
r\bigl(q(1-r)X-a(1-q+qr)Y\bigr)
-q(1-r)\bigl(rX-a(1-q+qr)Z\bigr)
+a(1-q+qr)\bigl(rY-q(1-r)Z\bigr)=0.
\]

**Reason.** Let

\[
B=k[a,q,r,X,Y,Z].
\]

The algebra is the Ore extension \(R=B[u;\delta]\), where

\[
\delta(a)=\delta(q)=\delta(r)=0,
\]
\[
\delta(X)=-\alpha,\qquad \delta(Y)=-\beta,\qquad \delta(Z)=-\gamma.
\]

If a central element had a positive power of \(u\), commuting it with \(Z\) would force its top coefficient to be killed by a nonzero multiple of \(r\), impossible in the domain \(B\). Hence every central element lies in \(B\).

So the center is exactly \(\ker \delta\subset B\). Up to sign, this is the kernel of

\[
D=\alpha\partial_X+\beta\partial_Y+\gamma\partial_Z.
\]

The elements

\[
\beta X-\alpha Y,\qquad \gamma X-\alpha Z,\qquad \gamma Y-\beta Z
\]

are visibly killed by \(D\). Also \(\gamma,\beta,\alpha\) form a regular sequence in \(k[a,q,r]\): modulo \(r\), \(\beta=q\), and then modulo \((r,q)\), \(\alpha=a\). For a constant-coefficient derivation with a regular coefficient triple, the invariant ring is generated by the base ring and the Koszul linear invariants above. Therefore no other central elements occur.
